RELIGION AND CREED — hate propaganda directed at Jews — poisoned atmosphere for Jews — conflict between expression of religious belief and right to be protected from discrimination based on religion — FREEDOM OF EXPRESSION — right to freely express opinion on any subject — HATE PROPAGANDA — exposure to hatred on basis of race or religion — DISCRIMINATION — adverse effect of discrimination — definition discrimination

EDUCATION — poisoned atmosphere at school — school board condoned discrimination — school board's liability for teacher's conduct — right to discipline teacher for off-duty conduct — students discriminated against on the basis of religious belief — impact of teacher's beliefs on students — teacher's right to freely express opinion on any subject — LIABILITY — employer liability — PUBLIC SERVICES AND FACILITIES — public school as public service — INTERPRETATION OF STATUTES — definition of school board as "person"

HUMAN RIGHTS — nature and purpose of human rights legislation — JURISDICTION — jurisdiction to hear complaint concerning issues governed by collective agreement — PARTIES — test for intervener status — complainant not person directly discriminated against — PROCEDURE — non-suit motion by respondent — REMEDIES — order to place employee on leave of absence without pay and terminate employment if discriminatory conduct continues

Summary:
The Board of Inquiry finds that the Board of School Trustees of District 15 discriminated against David Attis and his children by failing to take appropriate action in the case of Malcolm Ross, a teacher who made racist and bigoted statements in writing and in public fora regarding Jewish and other minority persons.

Malcolm Ross started teaching in District 15 in 1971. Between 1971 and this hearing Mr. Ross published several books alleging that the Holocaust was a hoax and warning readers against an international Jewish conspiracy. He also made numerous appearances to promote his discriminatory views.

David Attis is the parent of Yona Attis, a student in District 15 where Malcolm Ross teaches. His complaint has two elements. First, he alleges that Malcolm Ross has through statements and published writings made racist, discriminatory and bigoted statements that have led to a poisoned environment for Mr. Attis and his children in the educational services provided by District 15. Secondly, Mr. Attis alleges that by failing to properly discipline Malcolm Ross the Board of School Trustees has condoned Ross' views and further poisoned the atmosphere.

At the commencement of the hearing, the Board of Inquiry joins Malcolm Ross, the New Brunswick Teachers' Federation, the Department of Education, and the Canadian Jewish Congress as parties. The first three parties are joined because they may be directly affected by the outcome. The Board joins the Canadian Jewish Congress because of its ability to assist the inquiry by providing information. The Board of Inquiry has the power to join parties pursuant to s. 20.4(1) of the New Brunswick Human Rights Act, and it can make an order against any party found to have violated the
Act
.

Mr. Attis' complaint alleges that the Board of School Trustees breached s. 5 of the New Brunswick Human Rights Act by discriminating with respect to a public service. The courts addressed the policy issue of whether public education in public schools constitutes a public service and ruled that it is. The Board of Inquiry finds that the School Board is a "person" within the meaning of the
Act
, and that the School Board is liable for the actions of its employees.

The Board of Inquiry finds that s. 5 requires that the school environment including not just the formal school curricula, but also the informal exchange and participation must be non-discriminatory, and welcoming to students of all faiths and races.

In the complaint, there was reference to three incidents on school property in which Mr. Ross was alleged to have made discriminatory remarks to students and supply teachers between 1973 and 1976. However, the Board of Inquiry finds that there was no recent evidence of Mr. Ross making discriminatory remarks in the classroom and it did not give great weight to this aspect of the allegation.

On the other hand, the Board of Inquiry finds that there is ample evidence of Mr. Ross' discriminatory actions while off-duty, and that his off-duty conduct is relevant here. Teachers are role models for their students and their general conduct influences students. The Board of Inquiry finds that school boards have the right to discipline employees where the off-duty conduct has a negative effect on the employer's operation. The Board of Inquiry concludes that the public statements and writings of Malcolm Ross have, over many years, contributed to the creation of a poisoned environment within School District 15 and that this has interfered with the complainant's right to a non-discriminatory education for his children.

The Board of Inquiry also finds that the Board of School Trustees failed to take disciplinary actions available to it to curtail Mr. Ross' conduct and its negative effects on the students in the district. After clear warnings, Mr. Ross directly defied a school board instruction to abide by Department of Education policy regarding multiculturalism and human rights and the Board of School Trustees did not terminate his employment. Nor did the Board of Trustees take other actions to assist students negatively affected by the poisoned environment. The Board of School Trustees was reluctant to become involved in dealing with Malcolm Ross. The problems which Mr. Ross' activities created initially became evident in 1974. The Board of School Trustees reacted very slowly and when it did finally react in 1986 it did so ineffectually.

The Board of Inquiry orders the Department of Education to establish an annual review process which will set goals and assess progress in the implementation of its policy regarding multiculturalism and human rights. It also orders the Department of Education in collaboration with school trustees and teachers to establish a system for periodic assessment of race relations in the school environment. It orders the Board of School Trustees to immediately place Malcolm Ross on a leave of absence for eighteen months, to appoint him to a non-teaching position should one become available within this time, to terminate his employment immediately during the eighteen-month period or at any other time if he publishes or writes anything that mentions a Jewish or Zionist conspiracy or that attacks followers of the Jewish religion, and to terminate his employment if a non-teaching job is not available during the eighteen-month period or if he is offered a non-teaching job and refuses it.

The Board of Inquiry retains jurisdiction in case there are any difficulties encountered in the implementation of the award.

I.    BACKGROUND

[
1
]    This Board of Inquiry was established on September 1, 1988, pursuant to
s. 20
of the
Human Rights Act,
R.S.N.B. 1973, c. H-11 (the "
Act
") by the Honourable Mike McKee, Minister of Labour for the province of New Brunswick, to investigate the matter of a complaint of David Attis (the complainant) against Board of School Trustees, District 15 ("School Board"). Hearings into this matter were not able to commence until December 1990 due to several court challenges to the jurisdiction of the Board of Inquiry. Although these challenges in the courts did not significantly delay the commencement of the hearings of the Board of Inquiry, the decisions by the courts have assisted in answering many preliminary questions that would otherwise have been placed before this Board of Inquiry. The findings by the courts in relation to these preliminary questions will be referred to at relevant points in this decision.

[
2
]    The Board of Inquiry commenced hearings with the parties in December 1990 for eight days followed by fourteen days of hearings in April/May 1991. There were eleven witnesses called to give evidence. The proceedings have been transcribed and fill twenty-three volumes totalling 3,981 pages.

[
3
]    The complainant alleges that the School Board violated
s. 5
of the
Act
by discriminating against him and his children in the provision of accommodation, services or facilities on the basis of religion and ancestry.
Subsection 5(1)
of the
Act,
the relevant subsection, states as follows:

5. (1) No person, directly or indirectly, alone or with another, by himself or by the interposition of another, shall

(a)   deny to any person or class of persons any accommodation, services or facilities available to the public, or

(b)   discriminate against any person or class of persons with respect to any accommodation, services or facilities available to the public,

because of race, colour, religion, national origin, ancestry, place of origin, age, physical disability, mental disability, marital status or sex.

[
4
]    The complaint, dated April 21, 1988, alleges that the offence complained of occurred between March 29, 1977, through to April 21, 1988, the date the complaint was filed. The complaint reads as follows:

I am a Jew and three of my children are enrolled as students within District # 15.

I have reason to believe that Malcolm Ross, a teacher employed by the School Board, made racist, discriminatory and bigoted statements to his students during the 1976–77 school year. I have reason to believe that the School Board knew of this, yet it merely transferred Malcolm Ross to another school.

Malcolm Ross has written at least two books (i.e. Web of Deceit and Spectre of Power) and has made widely published statements (e.g.
Miramichi Leader,
October 22, 1986, page 5) that are anti-Jewish, racist, bigoted and discriminatory and that deny that six million Jews died during the Nazi Holocaust.

On April 22, 1987, the School Board failed to pass a motion condemning bigotry and racism. On March 15 or 16, 1988, Ray Maybee, a member of the School Board, publicly stated that Malcolm Ross' opinions were well documented and he had done his homework, thus appearing to support Mr. Ross' discriminatory views. Furthermore, when the School Board reprimanded Malcolm Ross on March 15, 1988, it referred to his views merely as controversial rather than discriminatory and the reprimand applied only to his future actions, not his past actions.

By its own statements and its inaction over Malcolm Ross' statements in class and in public, the School Board has condoned his views, has thus provided a racist and anti-Jewish role model for its students, has fostered a climate where students feel more at ease expressing anti-Jewish views, and has reduced the credibility of the content of its official history curriculum, thus depriving Jewish and other minority students of equal opportunity within the educational system that the School Board provides as a service to the public.

I believe that the School Board has thus furthered the aims of the Ross' of our society. I would like to give a couple of examples:

i)    Several students at the Magnetic Hill School intend to present a petition to the Premier of New Brunswick in support of Malcolm Ross. When asked if they concurred with Ross' views, the students replied that they didn't know.

ii)    My eldest daughter, a grade 6 student at Beaverbrook School was invited by a friend to attend a gymnastic exhibition at Magnetic Hill School. She was reminded by a classmate that she shouldn't go there because that is "where the teacher who hates Jews" works. She attended nevertheless.

I have reasonable cause to believe that the Board of School Trustees of District # 15 has violated Section 5 of the Human Rights Act.

Evidence as to events that occurred subsequent to April 21, 1988, was determined to be relevant and, therefore, admissible because the complaint was a continuing one and, further, because evidence as to what has occurred since the filing of the complaint may be necessary to determine what would be appropriate remedial action should the complaint be upheld.

[
5
]    The complainant, a lay person, drafted the complaint filed with the Human Rights Commission. Although the complaint may not be concise and clear in all respects, it does identify the basic nature of the complaint. The Saskatchewan Court of Queen's Bench
in the case of
Herman
and Rodin

(1989),
1989 CanLII 4505 (SK QB)
,
10 C.H.R.R. D/5798 (McLellan J.)
determined that proceedings before a board of inquiry under human rights legislation are civil rather than penal in nature. A complaint under human rights legislation, therefore, should not be subject to the same strict requirements as an information or indictment under the
Criminal Code
.
The purpose and objective of human rights legislation, which will be discussed at a later point, favours procedural flexibility versus procedural technicality provided there is no denial of natural justice. The New Brunswick Court of Appeal in its decision of September 8, 1989, reported at [
Board of Education of District 15
v.
Human Rights Board of Inquiry (N.B.)
]
(1989),
1989 CanLII 208 (NB CA)
,
100 N.B.R. (2d) 181
, [
(sub nom. New Brunswick (Human Rights Board of Inquiry)
v.
New Brunswick School Dist. No. 15),
10 C.H.R.R. D/6426] determined at 208 [at D/6432] that the complaint of David Attis met the statutory requirements of s. 17 of the
Act
and that if further information was required during the proceedings before the Board of Inquiry that a demand for particulars could be made. There was some correspondence between the School Board and the complainant prior to the commencement of the hearings regarding a demand for particulars but the matter was not pursued by the School Board or any of the other parties at the hearings before this Board of Inquiry.

[
6
]    The thrust of the complaint is that the School Board, by failing to take appropriate action against Malcolm Ross, a teacher working for the School Board who allegedly made racist, discriminatory and bigoted statements both to his students and in published statements and writings, has condoned an anti-Jewish role model and thus breached
s. 5
of the
Act
by discriminating against Jewish and other minority students within the educational system served by the School Board.

II.    PROCEDURAL MATTERS

[
7
]    The manner in which a board of inquiry may be established and its powers and method of proceeding are provided for in
s. 20
of the
Act
.
The Board is given very broad powers to determine its own method of procedure and is not bound by the rules of court. Several matters of a procedural nature arose during the conduct of the hearing requiring the Board to make rulings and give direction as to the process to be followed. Some of these rulings and directions will be summarized briefly in this section.

Designation of Parties

[
8
]    One of the most important decisions of a procedural nature made by this Board of Inquiry was the designation of parties prior to the commencement of hearings.
Subsection 20(4.1)
of the
Act
gives automatic party status to the Human Rights Commission (the "Commission"), the complainant and any person named in the complaint who is alleged to have violated the
Act.
In addition, para. (d) of
s. 20(4.1)
provides the Board of Inquiry with the power to designate any other person it may determine to be a party. Three additional parties were designated by the Board of Inquiry prior to the commencement of the hearings. These additional parties were Malcolm Ross, the New Brunswick Teachers' Federation (the "Teachers' Federation") and the Department of Education. These parties were designated because on an initial review of the complaint it was determined that all three had direct interests and rights which might be affected by an order of the Board of Inquiry if it was determined that a violation of the
Act
had occurred.
In
Re Damien and Ontario Human Rights Commission

(1976),
1976 CanLII 855 (ON HCJ)
,
12 O.R. (2d) 262 (Ont. Div.Ct.)
at 263,
Mr. Justice Osler concluded:

A party whose rights will be directly affected by the acts of a Court or administrative body should normally be a party to the proceedings contemplated.

[
9
]    Malcolm Ross's interests, as the teacher who allegedly made the statements and published writings to which objection was taken in the complaint and whom the School Board allegedly failed to discipline properly, are obvious. To find the School Board in breach of
s. 5(1)
for condoning the views of Malcolm Ross would possibly require imposing a remedy directly affecting Malcolm Ross. The complaint can also be read as claiming that the actions of Malcolm Ross are directly in breach of
s. 5(1)
because he is a teacher employed by the School Board. Counsel for Malcolm Ross at the commencement of the hearing stated that should the complaint be upheld his client could suffer severe consequences including possible loss of his teaching position.

[
10
]    The Teachers' Federation, as the bargaining representative of teachers in New Brunswick and as a party to the collective agreement governing the terms and conditions of employment between teachers and the School Board, has an interest in the proper application of the collective agreement and its relationship to the
Act
.
Finally, the Department of Education was added as a party upon the request of the School Board which claimed that the Department of Education played a vital role and had a vital interest in this matter. These three parties were given an opportunity at the commencement of the hearings of the Board of Inquiry to object to their designation as a party and none did so.

[
11
]    The Canadian Jewish Congress made application to the Board of Inquiry, prior to the commencement of the hearings, to be added as a party. The Board of Inquiry reserved decision on whether it would exercise its discretion to designate the Canadian Jewish Congress as a party and advised all parties who had been designated that this request from the Canadian Jewish Congress would be considered at the commencement of the hearings. The School Board and Malcolm Ross opposed this request from the Canadian Jewish Congress to be designated as a party. Written and oral submissions were received.

[
12
]    The general test that has been followed in deciding the issue of status in proceedings was
outlined by Esson J.A. in
MacMillan Bloedel Ltd.
v.
Mullin
; Martin
v.
British Columbia,

1985 CanLII 152 (BC CA)
,
[1985] 3 W.W.R. 380 (B.C.C.A.)
at 383
where he stated:

I do not mean to say that every application by a private or public interest group which can bring a different perspective to the issue should be allowed. I say only that, in some cases, that is a factor which will overcome the absence of a direct interest in the outcome. In each case, it will be necessary to consider the nature of the issue and the degree of likelihood that interveners will be able to make a useful contribution to the resolution of the issue without injustice to the immediate parties.

It is obvious from the comments by Mr. Justice Esson that the test for intervener status goes beyond the "direct interest" test to a more appropriate test of "useful contribution to the resolution of the issue without injustice to the immediate parties."

[
13
]    There is no challenge to the claim by the Canadian Jewish Congress that it does represent Canadian Jewry nor to its claim to a particular expertise and interest in the area of anti-Semitism and its manifestations which is the subject of the present complaint. This expertise and interest does allow the Canadian Jewish Congress to bring a different perspective to the Inquiry from that of any of the other parties. Another factor considered in deciding to add or exclude the Canadian Jewish Congress as a party to these proceedings was that the Canadian Jewish Congress was added as a party both at the Court of Queen's Bench and Court of Appeal levels in the New Brunswick cases which considered challenges to the right of this Board of Inquiry to proceed.

[
14
]    A further factor which must be considered in deciding to grant or deny party status is the nature of human rights legislation itself. The
Act
is remedial in nature and has as its objective the elimination of discrimination. It is important, given this objective, that all relevant views be presented and thus it is arguable that the
Act
allows for the process to be more open to interest groups with something to add to an inquiry. However, in deciding whether to add parties it is important to remember that the nature of the process is still an adversarial one and that all parties must be on a level playing field. To add parties would possibly affect the fairness of the process to a complainant and/or respondent. A respondent must be permitted to know the case it has to meet as presented by a complainant. To allow a third party to enter the picture at this initial level might be unfair in certain circumstances. As stated by Seaton J.A. in
Canada (A.G.)
v.
Aluminum Co. of Canada

(1987),
1987 CanLII 162 (BC CA)
,
10 B.C.L.R. (2d) 371
at 385
:

Interveners should not be permitted to take the litigation away from those directly affected by it. Parties to litigation should be allowed to define the issues and seek resolution of matters they determine appropriate to place in issue. They should not be compelled to deal with issues raised by others.

[
15
]    This Board of Inquiry is of the opinion that there is no fundamental difference in the position which would be advanced by the Canadian Jewish Congress and the complainant. However, there is sufficient indication that there may be a difference in perspective regarding the issue in dispute. It is
noted that the
Canadian Jewish Congress
has given sufficient advance notice to the other parties of its intention to seek party status.

[
16
]    After a full consideration of the above factors, the Board of Inquiry determined that the Canadian Jewish Congress should be permitted to become a party to the proceedings for purposes of legal argument only. The Canadian Jewish Congress was not permitted to call or cross-examine witnesses.

[
17
]    There is confusion amongst some members of the public on the role of a board of inquiry appointed under s. 20 of the
Act
and the right of members of the public to make submissions to a board of inquiry on the general topic area of the complaint. The role of the board of inquiry by s. 20(1) is specifically limited to the investigation of the matter complained of following the failure of the Commission to settle the matter. The name "board of inquiry" suggests a proceeding more in the nature of a royal commission or public inquiry into matters which are not governed by statute. The matter complained of relates to a specific allegation of a breach of the
Act
by a named person.
Subsection 20(6.1)
states that at the conclusion of the inquiry, if the board does not find, on a balance of probabilities, that the
Act
has been violated, the board shall dismiss the complaint. If a conclusion is made that the
Act
has been violated then the board is provided with a range of powers to effect compliance and rectify any harm. It is an adversarial process in which parties are specifically identified by the
Act
(the complainant, respondent and Commission) with power in the Board, as noted earlier, to add parties. The onus is on the complainant to prove that a violation of the
Act
has occurred. In such circumstances, it is essential that the rules of natural justice be respected in the proceedings of the board of inquiry. Although a board of inquiry is given the power to establish its own procedure, to stray far from the traditional rules applicable to court proceedings is to risk denying a party a fair hearing. This Board of Inquiry, therefore, has limited itself to the specifics of the complaint before it and has only considered evidence presented during the hearings at which all parties had the opportunity to be present.

Non-Suit Motion

[
18
]    Upon close of the complainant's case, counsel for Malcolm Ross moved a motion of non-suit based on there being no evidence, presented by the complainant, upon which the Board could rule or exercise its jurisdiction under the
Act
.
The motion was joined in by counsel for the School Board, counsel for the Department of Education and counsel for the Teachers' Federation. Counsel for the complainant opposed the appropriateness of such a motion.

[
19
]    In raising the motion, concern was expressed by counsel for Malcolm Ross and counsel for the Teachers' Federation as to whether the parties moving the motion would be permitted to elect to call evidence, if the motion was defeated. The Board of Inquiry agreed it would not foreclose the option of an election in its consideration of the motion. This Board's consideration of the motion, therefore, involved two possible steps. Firstly, it had to consider the appropriateness of such a motion being before it and, secondly, if it was determined appropriate, the Board had to make a determination on the merits of the motion. If the motion was found to be inappropriate, a decision on the merits would not be made in order to preserve the option, as requested by counsel for the Teachers' Federation, to elect to call evidence. It was not disputed by counsel for the complainant that a party should have the option of moving a motion of non-suit if such motion is coupled with an election not to call evidence.

[
20
]    In considering the motion of non-suit the Board of Inquiry has reviewed decisions from other boards of inquiry, case law precedents, academic writings and submissions of counsel for the respective parties. This Board has concluded that non-suit motions, without election not to call evidence, while appropriate in certain circumstances before boards of inquiry, will be infrequent and rare and that the generally acceptable approach will be for parties moving such motions to be required to elect to call evidence.

[
21
]    In
Ontario Human Rights Commission and
Abary
v.
North York Branson Hospital
and Hull

(1988),
1988 CanLII 8885 (ON HRT)
,
9 C.H.R.R. D/4975 (Ratushny)
, a decision of a board of inquiry established under the
Human Rights Code
of Ontario, Mr. Ratushny states at para. 38201 [D/4975]:

. . . an application in the nature of "no case to meet" should be permitted before administrative tribunals without requiring the respondent first to elect whether or not to call evidence.

However, Mr. Ratushny goes on to state at para. 38203: " . . . a ruling of ”˜no case to meet' is likely to be infrequent before boards of inquiry." Mr. Ratushny, at para. 38202,
in
Abary
emphasizes the point that the threshold is " . . . very low, i.e. ”˜any' evidence capable of supporting the adverse finding." Further he points out that it is important that no decision as to the credibility of the evidence is being made at this point in time. He states, again at para. 38202, that the credibility of the evidence will only be weighed where the " . . . testimony . . . is so far-fetched as not to be capable of belief by any reasonable person."

[
22
]    This Board of Inquiry has reviewed several decisions from courts in Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, and Newfoundland concerning the procedure to be followed in civil proceedings. The courts in many of these cases permitted argument to proceed on a motion for non-suit without requiring the parties to elect not to call evidence. However, also without exception, all of these jurisdictions had rules of civil procedure which allowed the parties to have their motion considered without putting them to an election. No such rule has been discovered in New Brunswick.
See:
Campbell
v.
Campbell (No. 1)

(1990),
1989 CanLII 4990 (NL SC)
,
83 Nfld. & P.E.I.R. 332
;
Robichaud
v.
Bruce

(1988),
1988 CanLII 9651 (NS CA)
,
83 N.S.R. (2d) 280
;
Manuel Estate
v.
Parsons Estate,

[1991] N.J. No. 37
[unreported]
;
Ward
v.
Harris Projects Ltd.

(1989),
1988 CanLII 8810 (PE SCTD)
,
73 Nfld. & P.E.I.R. 11
. Further, in reaching its conclusion this Board referred to M.R. Gorsky's summary in his text
Evidence and Procedure in Canadian Labour Arbitration
(Don Mills, Ont.: R. De Boo, 1981) at p. 237 in which he states that it is customary for parties in labour arbitrations to be put to an election before consideration of a non-suit motion by the arbitrator. It is noted that labour arbitration boards, like this Board of Inquiry, are not subject to the civil rules of procedure and that many similarities exist between boards of arbitration and boards of inquiry in the goals and objectives sought to be met by these processes.

[
23
]    The issue of the proper procedure to be followed when dealing with non-suit motions is also extensively discussed in a 1985 decision by H.A. Hubbard,
Nimako
v.
CN Hotels

(1985),
1985 CanLII 5248 (ON HRT)
,
6 C.H.R.R. D/2894
. This case dealt with a motion of non-suit by a respondent and it was subsequently decided that the respondent should either withdraw the motion or elect to call no evidence. In reaching this conclusion, Professor Hubbard cited
Oxford
v.
Department of Health and Social Security,
[1977] I.C.R. 884 as authority for the proposition that the respondent should be put to an election. At para. 23568 [D/2896], Hubbard quotes Phillips J. at pp. 886–7:

It further seems to us that, while the burden of proof lies upon the applicant, it would only be in
exceptional or frivolous
cases that it would be right for the industrial tribunal to find at the end of the applicant's case that there was no case to answer and that it was not necessary to hear what the respondent had to say about it. [Emphasis added.]

Further, Professor Hubbard states, at para. 23569 [D/2897]:

No one participating in a hearing can fail to form impressions as the evidence is being adduced; but until arguments are heard and duly considered it would seem improper to make a
finding
that the Commission's case is "weak" and that
therefore
the Respondent may pursue a non-suit motion without having to elect to call no evidence.

Finally, concerning the issue of the procedure to be followed concerning non-suit motions, Professor Hubbard, at para. 23569 [D/2897] states:

The view I have come to is that,
unless there is something exceptional in the circumstances before it
, a Board of Inquiry under the
Human Rights Code
ought not to entertain a non-suit motion without putting the respondent to an election . . . [Emphasis added.]

Professor Hubbard characterized proceedings, at paras. 23566–67 [D/2896], before a board of inquiry as analogous to civil proceedings and saw a distinction in the manner in which non-suit motions should be addressed in a civil proceeding and in a criminal proceeding. He referred, at para. 23559 [D/2894], to
Re Cedarvale Tree Services Ltd. and Labourers' International Union of North America, Local 183

(1972),
1971 CanLII 341 (ON CA)
,
22 D.L.R. (3d) 40
at 49,
as authority for the proposition that an inquiry may " . . . adopt such procedure as appears to it to be
just and convenient
in the particular circumstances of the case before it." [Emphasis added.]

[
24
]    This Board accepts the reasoning of Professor Hubbard regarding the nature of inquiries being civil in nature, albeit with more flexibility than might be found in the normal civil proceeding. As well, his reasoning is persuasive regarding the need for boards of inquiry to consider what is "just and convenient" in determining how the process should be implemented. With regard to the present case, it was determined that it was not appropriate for the motion for dismissal without election to be considered given the circumstances of this case and the public nature of this inquiry. As noted earlier, the Board was asked not to pre-empt the right of certain parties to elect not to call evidence and thus restricted its ruling to the appropriateness of the motion in terms of process. As it was found to be an inappropriate motion, it was not a motion that could properly come before it to be considered on its merits and the Board ruled the motion be withdrawn. No party to the original motion exercised its option to put forth a new motion of non-suit in which it was prepared to elect not to call evidence.

III.    EVIDENCE

[
25
]    Before proceeding to discuss the evidence it is appropriate to make a few brief comments concerning the manner in which the evidence is to be presented. Only that evidence most relevant to the issue being decided by this Board has been summarized. For ease of analysis the evidence has been divided into the following four categories: employment record of Malcolm Ross; writings and statements by Malcolm Ross; School Board's actions; and, alleged effects.

Employment Record of Malcolm Ross

[
26
]    Malcolm Ross, as evidenced by the employment record supplied by the School Board and background information supplied in the Review Committee report of February 25, 1987, was employed as a teacher at Birchmount School from September 1, 1971, to June 1976 and at Magnetic Hill School from September 30, 1976, to the present. Both of these schools are in School District 15. Malcolm Ross is currently a modified resource teacher at Magnetic Hill School and teaches approximately thirteen students per day for varying periods of time. Malcolm Ross does not have a homeroom class.

Writings and Statements by Malcolm Ross

[
27
]    The evidence presented to the Inquiry shows that Malcolm Ross has written and authorized publication of a number of books which have been the subject of complaint and/or controversy. These include (listed by copyright date):

1.
Web of Deceit
— copyright 1978;

2.
The Real Holocaust (The Attack on Unborn Children and        Life Itself)
— copyright 1983;

3.
Spectre of Power
— copyright 1987;

4.
Christianity vs. Judeo-Christianity (The Battle for Truth)
— copyright 1987, 4th printing 1989.

In addition to his published works, Malcolm Ross has written a number of letters to the editors of various papers in New Brunswick, including (listed in chronological order):

1. Letter to the editor —
The Moncton Times
— February 22,        1978;

2. Letter to the editor —
The Daily Gleaner
— June 6, 1983;

3. Letter to the editor —
The Miramichi Leader
— October 22,        1986.

There was no evidence presented which contradicted the authorship of either the letters or the books as being that of Malcolm Ross. Further, the Inquiry was presented with evidence that Malcolm Ross appeared on a local television program on November 21, 1989, in which he discussed his views and the books which he had written.

School Board's Actions

[
28
]    Evidence, although hearsay, was presented that Malcolm Ross had uttered racist comments about "blacks in Rhodesia" while he was teaching at Birchmount School during the early to mid-1970s. Some of these comments were allegedly made in the classroom. Reference to these remarks can be found in the testimony of David Attis; in a letter to Ross McCallum from Charles Devona, dated February 3, 1987; in submissions to the Review Committee which was established in 1987; and, in
Spectre of Power
(at p. 112).

[
29
]    The evidence indicates that the publications of Malcolm Ross were causing public comment as early as 1978 and that the School Board was aware of the controversy during that year. A review of the evidence shows that Julius Israeli contacted the School Board, through letters to the Director of School District 15 and the Principal of Magnetic Hill School, regarding his concerns about Malcolm Ross and his continued employment. In fact, Julius Israeli requested that the School Board dismiss Malcolm Ross. These letters were dated April 26, 1978, May 9, 1978, and another on May 17, 1978.

[
30
]    In addition to the above letters, the School Board had been contacted by Noel Kinsella, Chairman of the Human Rights Commission, in a letter of June 12, 1978. In the letter Noel Kinsella expressed concern over the writings of Malcolm Ross and requested that the classroom performance of Malcolm Ross be supervised. As well, in a May 17, 1978, article in
The North Shore Leader,
it was noted that Malcolm Ross had been the subject of an ATV commentary by Gary McCauley. While the commentary apparently did not mention Malcolm Ross or his book,
Web of Deceit,
by name, the article makes it clear that Malcolm Ross was the subject of the commentary. The article cites Reverend Gary McCauley as calling for the dismissal of Malcolm Ross and rejecting the right of Malcolm Ross to publish his writings under the protection of a right to free speech. Also in 1978, at least two articles appeared in the Moncton area newspaper,
The Moncton Transcript,
dealing with the issue. It is noted that in an article of June 2, 1978, Noel Kinsella referred to the importance of protecting free speech versus suppressing the work of Malcolm Ross on the basis that it might cause discrimination. The article was written in relation to the publication of the book,
Web of Deceit,
and included comments from a member of the Jewish community and the School Board. Rabbi Stanley Greenberg expressed the view that the book had caused members of the Jewish community to become upset because of its being anti-Jewish and an improper portrayal of Zionism. Further, the article stated that Julius Israeli had been attempting to have Malcolm Ross dismissed and to have the Justice Department review this work in light of hate literature laws. Also, the article noted that Nancy Humphrey, Chairperson of the School Board at that time, stated the School Board's position as being that Malcolm Ross could do what he wanted on his own time. Also in 1978, Malcolm Ross and Julius Israeli wrote letters to the editor of
The Moncton Times
in which they each accused the other of distorting "the facts."

[
31
]    From 1979 up to and including 1984 there is little evidence of a public controversy concerning Malcolm Ross and his views. The evidence shows that Malcolm Ross's in-class teaching was being monitored at least for part of this time. In 1983, a letter by Malcolm Ross to the editor of
The Daily Gleaner
prompted the Human Rights Commission to contact the Superintendent of School District 15 to ensure that Malcolm Ross's activities were still being monitored. By 1986, the Malcolm Ross issue was again being addressed by various articles, letters, and other media coverage. The media coverage at this time, according to Carl Ross, Chairman of the School Board, caused the School Board to begin to spend a lot of time on the issue. The testimony of Carl Ross further revealed that by 1986–87, the School Board was receiving approximately ten to twenty letters per week on the issue. Further, the evidence shows meetings between representatives of the School Board and Malcolm Ross during this time.

[
32
]    On October 22, 1986, Malcolm Ross wrote a letter to the editor of
The Miramichi Leader
outlining his views. This letter is very relevant because it provides a clear summary of Malcolm Ross's opinions and dispels any uncertainties as to the interpretation to be placed on his earlier writings. Following this letter, School Board representatives met with Malcolm Ross on November 18, 1986. A follow-up letter from the School Board, dated November 26, 1986, shows that the meeting was held to discuss concerns over articles which had appeared in the media and contacts made with the School Board by the Departments of Justice and Education. The letter reveals that it was agreed that a monitoring scheme would be established in which Malcolm Ross's classroom would be visited "at least three times a week" and the materials being used in class by Malcolm Ross would be reviewed.

[
33
]    Also in 1986, a copy of a letter addressed to Julius Israeli from David Clark, the Attorney General of New Brunswick at the time, was published. In the letter, Mr. Clark refused to pursue legal action against Malcolm Ross under the hate literature laws of the
Criminal Code
of Canada. Further, an article by Don Hoyt of
The Telegraph-Journal
on December 17, 1986, highlighted the public interest in Malcolm Ross's works by reporting the views of a number of individuals who had spoken out against Malcolm Ross and his views.

[
34
]    By 1987, the controversy over Malcolm Ross's writings was increasing both in the level of the School Board's involvement and in the public response to the entire issue. A number of news clippings appeared in various newspapers across the province. These news clippings largely dealt with the controversy over the possible prosecution of Malcolm Ross under the hate literature laws. They did, however, reflect a concern about the possible discriminatory effect of Malcolm Ross's views. Expressions of concern were also being received by the School Board from a number of people during 1987. Generally, the tone of the letters was one which called upon the School Board to act concerning Malcolm Ross. Further, the Department of Education was also actively involved in the Malcolm Ross issue during 1987.

[
35
]    Presumably in response to expressions of concern, the School Board decided to investigate the issue and its possible impact upon the school system. In a motion of January 28, 1987, the School Board established a Review Committee to " . . . review the possible impact of this issue upon the learning environment in school programs." Further, the School Board went on record at the same time to express its concern that the issue had the potential to cause harm to " . . . the positive human relations that are essential to the well being of a community . . ." The Review Committee interpreted its mandate as being a determination of how Malcolm Ross's personal views might, if at all, be affecting the delivery of the school curriculum and in what ways, if any, the positive human relations of the school community were being affected by the publicity surrounding the Malcolm Ross issue. In addition, however, the Review Committee defined "community" as including only the Magnetic Hill School community rather than all of School District 15. The School Board accepted the Committee's report on February 25, 1987. The Committee's findings, at p. 8, were:

1.    That there appears to be no evidence to suggest that Malcolm Ross is teaching his beliefs or discussing his religious theories with staff or students.

2.    That there is not [
sic
] evidence to suggest that the publicity surrounding Malcolm Ross has had a negative effect on the human relations within the present school or between the school and the community.

The Committee's report does not make mention of a letter addressed to the Superintendent of School District 15 dated February 3, 1987, from Charles Devona alleging that Malcolm Ross had expressed racist comments in class while at Birchmount School. Nor does the report in its conclusions address the issues raised in the substantial and well written submission to the Committee from the Atlantic Jewish Council concerning Malcolm Ross's views and their possible discriminatory effect. Finally, although the report lists allegations by two former teachers who had worked with Malcolm Ross that he had made comments of a racist nature while at Birchmount School, they are not referred to in its findings.

[
36
]    With regard to the Review Committee, its process, and its findings, counsel for the complainant called Ernest Hodgson as an expert witness in the field of education. This Board of Inquiry accepts Ernest Hodgson as an expert witness in the field of education but notes that his relevant experience was not recent experience and that this fact has influenced the weight that this Board of Inquiry is prepared to give to it. Further, some of his evidence falls within the realm of common understanding and has little value as expert evidence. He testified that the Review Committee was flawed in its composition, processes used, and that the Committee failed to discharge the mandate given to it by the School Board. Ernest Hodgson claimed that the composition of the Committee was flawed in that the Committee should have had a majority of independent members. Ernest Hodgson testified that the Committee had flawed the process by rejecting expert advice as to the conducting of interviews, by conducting fifty-nine interviews in four days, by reading out two rather detailed questions and asking for a response, and by improperly selecting the interview sample. Ernest Hodgson stated:

If you get the original questions wrong and you get the processes wrong and then you get the answers wrong, and then the answers misinterpreted, then the whole thing is wrong.

Finally, he believed that the Committee had misinterpreted its mandate by only addressing the impact of Malcolm Ross's activities on the learning programs at Magnetic Hill School rather than the entire school district. In this regard, he also saw the Committee as improperly focussing on the publicity surrounding Malcolm Ross rather than upon any actual negative effect within the school and community. In essence then, Ernest Hodgson testified that the results of the report were unreliable in that the Committee failed to fully investigate and examine the implications of the alleged private actions of Malcolm Ross.

[
37
]    September 17, 1987, saw the first direct meeting between Malcolm Ross and the Chairman of the School Board. Carl Ross testified that he believed the meeting came about so that both parties could come to a clearer understanding of their respective positions. At this meeting, the publications of Malcolm Ross were discussed. In a letter dated April 26, 1988, Cheryl Reid, acting Superintendent at the time, states that Malcolm Ross was " . . . cautioned strongly against any further publications regarding [his] views . . ." at the meeting between Carl Ross, Cheryl Reid, Betty Lutes and Malcolm Ross. In response to disciplinary action related to the publication of his book,
Spectre of Power,
in late 1987 or early 1988, Malcolm Ross claimed that the School Board at the September 17, 1987, meeting had given "tacit approval" for the publication of this book.

[
38
]    Also in 1987, two motions proposed by Audrey Lampert concerning the Ross issue failed due to a lack of a seconder. These motions dealt with the release of the Review Committee report and with the School Board making a public statement rejecting all forms of racism and hatemongering.

[
39
]    The first significant event of 1988 was the imposition of disciplinary action against Malcolm Ross. The evidence shows that the School Board decided in March 1988 that Malcolm Ross had inhibited its ability to manage and direct the educational process and had detrimentally affected its reputation. It also noted a negative impact in Malcolm Ross's reputation and his perceived inability to foster an atmosphere of tolerance as a public school teacher. Therefore, by letter of March 16, 1988, in which the School Board referred to his writings as controversial, Malcolm Ross was informed that any further publications, or public discussion of his views or his works, would lead to greater disciplinary action, including the possibility of dismissal. The School Board also stated to Malcolm Ross that compliance with its directives would result in the matter being considered closed. Malcolm Ross grieved this decision without success. He disputed that the School Board's abilities were negatively affected or that the School Board's reputation had been adversely affected. It was shortly before the imposition of this disciplinary action that an opinion letter from Clyde Spinney, counsel to the School Board at that time, indicated that the School Board could discipline for out-of-school conduct. The reprimand and restriction, sometimes referred to as the "gag order," of March 16, 1988, was kept in Malcolm Ross's personal file until September 20, 1989, when it was ordered removed.

[
40
]    The next relevant action of 1988 was the filing of three complaints concerning the Malcolm Ross issue. On March 18, 1988, Kathleen Makela filed a complaint against the Board of School Trustees, District 15, alleging discrimination, as per s. 5 of the
Human Rights Act,
on the basis of ancestry and religion. Kathleen Makela also filed a complaint on April 20, 1988, in which she alleged a breach of s. 6 of the
Human Rights Act.
On April 21, 1988, David Attis filed the complaint which is the subject of the present Inquiry. Kathleen's Makela's complaints were withdrawn and dismissed later in 1988.

[
41
]    Subsequent to the above complaints being filed, the Human Rights Commission began its investigation. As part of this investigation the Human Rights Commission requested the School Board to release records concerning Malcolm Ross, his students, and a copy of the Review Committee Report. In addition, the Commission made two settlement offers which do not appear to have been pursued by the School Board. The School Board refused to release the requested documentation to the Commission on the basis that it wished to protect the confidentiality of teachers' records, that it was concerned over the possible identification of special needs students, and that it was concerned because of the confidential nature of the Review Committee Report. This refusal was outlined in a letter of August 25, 1988, from Carl Ross to Francis Young of the Human Rights Commission. Upon the failure of the parties to resolve the complaint, the Commission recommended that this Board of Inquiry be established and on September 1, 1988, the Minister of Labour, the Honourable Mike McKee, complied with this recommendation.

[
42
]    During 1988 the School Board continued to monitor the in-class activities of Malcolm Ross. Further, the School Board was made aware of views both in favour of and opposed to Malcolm Ross. These ranged from expressions of dissatisfaction with Malcolm Ross by individuals such as Premier Frank McKenna and Education Minister Shirley Dysart, to a filing of a complaint with the Human Rights Commission by Charles Simon Puxley, concerning what he considered to be the unjust treatment of Malcolm Ross. By this point in time the Attorney General, James Lockyer, had announced that no charges would be laid against Malcolm Ross under the hate literature laws. Also, 1988 saw the development by the Department of Education of a Holocaust curriculum and a report on "Initiatives in Multicultural Education" describing various programs dealing with multiculturalism.

[
43
]    On March 22, 1989, the School Board adopted Policy 5006 which established guidelines for teachers regarding individual rights and freedoms. This policy was intended to ensure that students were provided with a positive and safe learning environment which taught respect for individuals' rights and freedoms. This policy also provided for disciplinary action in the event that any employee's actions constituted a hindrance to the provision of school services. In August 1989, the Minister of Education released a ministerial statement on Multicultural/Human Rights Education which was intended to set the direction for policy development by school boards to ensure that multicultural and human rights education formed " . . . an integral part of [the] school system."

[
44
]    On September 20, 1989, the School Board decided to remove the reprimand and restriction from Malcolm Ross's file and asked Malcolm Ross to comply with the provisions of Policy 5006. This decision and request were communicated to Malcolm Ross in a letter of September 22, 1989. Further, the School Board again informed Malcolm Ross that some of his past actions and comments had affected the administrative operation of Magnetic Hill School and had caused some parents to be concerned about general safety and the attention being brought to the school. On November 21, 1989, approximately two months after the removal of the restriction and reprimand from Malcolm Ross's file, Malcolm Ross appeared on a local television program. This decision was communicated to Malcolm Ross in a letter of December 1, 1989. In this letter, Ross MacCallum, on behalf of the School Board, characterized Malcolm Ross's actions and the School Board's request in the following manner:

The School Board is sincerely requesting that you refrain from
publicly assailing
another religious belief, the Jewish religion, when proclaiming your own faith. [Emphasis added.]

and

In the view of the School Board, your current approach to the method of expounding upon your religious beliefs by
publicly denouncing
another borders on freedom or licence to judge and condemn . . . [Emphasis added.]

[
45
]    In a related letter of December 1, 1989, the School Board requested the Department of Education to provide input as to whether Malcolm Ross's appearance constituted a breach of the ministerial statement of 1989. Rather, it was meant to provide a guideline to school boards so that they might develop their own policies. Further, the letter stated that day-to-day responsibility for disciplinary action lay with the School Board.

Alleged Effects

[
46
]    The evidence reveals that there were many incidents in which Jewish students were singled out, either in school activities or by other students, and made to feel different. For the purposes of this section of the decision, the evidence of Yona Attis and Leigh Lampert will figure most prominently. The evidence of David Attis regarding incidents against Jewish students is for the most part hearsay and therefore cannot be given the same weight.

[
47
]    Before proceeding to review the evidence of Yona Attis and Leigh Lampert, some comments concerning the testimony of young witnesses in general, and the testimony of these two students in particular, is warranted. It is important to remember that testifying at any hearing is often difficult even for adults, especially during cross-examination. However, if a witness's evidence is to be given full weight it is important that the testimony be able to stand up to cross-examination. While it is true that the testimony of Yona Attis was punctuated with periods of strong emotionalism, it is also equally true that the evidence was presented in a credible and forthright manner, as was the evidence of Leigh Lampert. This Board accepts the evidence of Yona Attis and Leigh Lampert and given the length of time over which many of the incidents to which they referred occurred, the Board believes that the evidence was presented in a manner consistent with the passage of time.

[
48
]    One of the first incidents referred to by Yona Attis in her testimony occurred in the spring of 1988 when she went to watch a gymnastic competition at Magnetic Hill School. Yona Attis testified that her friends, upon hearing that she was going to be attending the competition at Magnetic Hill School, told her that she could not go there because that was " . . . where the teacher who hates Jews works." Another friend stated that the teacher's name was Malcolm Ross. After this, Yona Attis testified that she went to the school but that the whole time she was there she was scared " . . . that someone was going to come up behind me and grab me and beat me up or something." Upon cross-examination, Yona Attis stated that she believed she would continue to have fear if she was to enter Magnetic Hill School because of the presence of Malcolm Ross at the school.

[
49
]    Yona Attis testified that as early as grade two she could remember a supply teacher at Edith Cavell School asking the students in her class to raise their hands if they loved Jesus. She claimed that she felt different because only herself and one other did not put up their hands. Starting in grade five a number of incidents began to occur. These ranged from name-calling based on her religion, to the wearing of swastikas by some students, to the drawing of swastikas on her books and school bag. While in the earlier years, these events were caused by a small number of students in the school, in later years, such as when Yona Attis was transferred back to Edith Cavell School, as many as twenty students, at one time or another, participated. Another aspect of this taunting was the shouting and signalling of the "Heil, Hitler" salute in her presence. Further, Yona Attis testified that she was made to feel different when various entertainers would come to the school and promote their Christian beliefs. Two particular incidents which stood out in her mind involved in the one instance, a keyboard player and, in the other instance, basketball players who professed their belief in Christianity. She testified that she was upset and although she felt like walking out during these incidents she did not for fear of standing out. Yona Attis testified that as far as she was concerned the teachers and principal did not really attempt to do anything about her situation. Yona Attis testified that she had suffered greatly as a result of all the name-calling, the drawing and wearing of swastikas, and the apparent unwillingness of school officials to do anything to resolve the situation.

[
50
]    The evidence of Leigh Lampert indicates that he experienced incidents similar to those of Yona Attis while attending school in School District 15. It is evident that the wearing of swastikas and the drawing of swastikas on blackboards, walls, and books was also happening. Leigh Lampert also testified that a supply teacher, together with another student, gave the "Heil, Hitler" salute while in class.

[
51
]    With regard to the testimony of the other students all that needs to be said is that it generally supported the testimony of Yona Attis.

[
52
]    Yona Attis testified that her image of Malcolm Ross was created both by the media and perhaps by her father. Leigh Lampert also testified that his image of Malcolm Ross was largely determined by what he had heard from various media and from discussions at home. He further testified that he had read portions of
Spectre of Power
and had determined, for himself, that the book was anti-Semitic.

[
53
]    The testimony of David Attis indicated that he was a parent who was very concerned about the type of education his children would receive and how the presence of Malcolm Ross might affect this education. David Attis testified that he was concerned about the emotional drain on his daughter because of the various incidents which had occurred at school. He expressed his apprehension that his other daughters would also face discrimination within the school system because they were Jewish. Finally, David Attis testified that Yona Attis had informed him that the teachers did nothing to prevent the various attacks on her while she was at school.

[
54
]    There can be no doubt that David Attis sincerely believes that the writings and publications of Malcolm Ross are anti-Jewish, racist, bigoted and discriminatory. David Attis acknowledged that he had very little direct contact with the School Board on this issue prior to the complaint being filed on April 21, 1988. He maintained that this was so because he had become disillusioned with the process by which the School Board had handled complaints of discrimination in the past. Further, he believes that the School Board condoned Malcolm Ross's views by failing to act and to condemn those views. He is of the opinion that the School Board has, in effect, created a discriminatory environment within which Jewish students cannot be treated equally.

[
55
]    Ernest Hodgson, in discussing the potential for impact upon the school system of Malcolm Ross's views, testified that this type of issue could not help but manifest itself in the relations within the school and between the school and the community at large. Of particular concern to Ernest Hodgson was the impact upon children of a teacher's outside activities. In the present case, Ernest Hodgson believed that Malcolm Ross's views and his public dissemination thereof, was certain to have an impact upon Jewish children. He held that teachers can have a great impact upon the students they teach. In this regard, he referred to a number of codes of ethics and/or teaching codes from across the country which dealt with the conduct expected of teachers. His opinion was that these codes reveal the need for teachers not to undermine the confidence or security of their students.

[
56
]    With regard to the position of Jewish students within the school system, it was his opinion that the situation was one in which the students, having a general knowledge of Malcolm Ross, could be fearful and otherwise afraid of Malcolm Ross. Further, he stated it was possible that Jewish students would be negatively influenced and would consider themselves the subject of suspicion or distrust and isolated from their friends. As well, it was possible that there would be a reluctance on the part of Jewish parents to participate within the school system and that Malcolm Ross's views could also discourage other Jewish parents from moving to the Moncton area.

IV.    DECISION

General Principles of Interpretation Applicable to Human Rights Legislation

[
57
]    The courts, in interpreting human rights legislation, have placed great emphasis on the unique nature and objectives of such legislation as reflected not only in the substantive provisions but also in the preamble which is a common feature of most human rights legislation. The courts in support of the general objectives of human rights legislation have given the various specific provisions within the legislation a broad rather than narrow application. Mr. Justice McIntyre in the Supreme Court of Canada decision
Ontario Human Rights Commission and O'Malley
v.
Simpsons-Sears
Ltd.,

1985 CanLII 18 (SCC)
,
[1985] 2 S.C.R. 536
[7 C.H.R.R. D/3102], at pp. 546–47 [D/3105, para. 24766], summarized this broad purposive approach to the interpretation of human rights legislation as follows:

It is not, in my view, a sound approach to say that according to established rules of construction no broader meaning can be given to the
Code
than the narrowest interpretation of the words employed. The accepted rules of construction are flexible enough to enable the Court to recognize in the construction of a human rights code the special nature and purpose of the enactment . . . and give to it an interpretation which will advance its broad purposes. Legislation of this type is of a special nature, not quite constitutional but certainly more than the ordinary — and it is for the courts to seek out its purpose and give it effect. The
Code
aims at the removal of discrimination.

Chief Justice Stratton in the New Brunswick Court of Appeal decision [
Board of Education of District 15
],
supra,
at p. 201 [D/6431, para. 45415] cites further Supreme Court of Canada decisions which support his purposive approach:

The purposive approach in construing human rights statutes has been followed by the Supreme Court of Canada in
Canadian National Railway Co.
v.
Bhinder,

1985 CanLII 19 (SCC)
,
[1985] 2 S.C.R. 561
;
Action Travail des Femmes
v.
Canadian National Railway Co.,

1987 CanLII 109 (SCC)
,
[1987] 1 S.C.R. 1114
; 76 N.R. 161, and
Brennan
v.
Canada and Robichaud,

1987 CanLII 73 (SCC)
,
[1987] 2 S.C.R. 84
; 75 N.R. 303 . . .

[
58
]    The general objective of the
Act
is a fundamental one — that of fostering respect and equal treatment for all persons without regard to the individual's race, colour, religion, national origin, ancestry, place of origin, age, physical disability, mental disability, marital status or sex. Differential treatment of individuals on these grounds often results from prejudices that are deep-rooted and ingrained in our society. Assisting individuals through education and public awareness to identify and recognize their prejudices and the unfairness of judging others on the basis of these prejudices is seen as one of the long-term solutions to eliminating discrimination. At the same time, however, in addition to its objective of eliminating discriminatory conduct generally, human rights legislation has identified specific areas in which discriminatory conduct is prohibited. For example,
s. 3
of the
Act
prohibits discrimination in the hiring or continuing employment of individuals;
s. 4
prohibits discrimination in the rental and sale of housing and property;
s. 5
prohibits discrimination with respect to any accommodation, services or facilities available to the public;
s. 6
prohibits the publication of certain notices, signs, symbols or emblems that discriminate against any person; and, s. 7 prevents the exclusion of individuals on discriminatory grounds from professional associations or business or trade associations. The
Act,
with respect to these areas of discrimination, provides relief to those who have been the subject of the discrimination.

[
59
]    The courts have also now clearly established that it is the effect of the complainant and not the intent of the party accused of discriminating which is relevant in determining whether the human rights legislation has been breached. Mr. Justice McIntyre
in the
Simpsons-Sears
case,
supra,
at p. 547 [D/3105, para. 24766] commented as follows:

It is the result or the effect of the action complained of which is significant. If it does, in fact, cause discrimination; if its effect is to impose on one person or group of persons obligations, penalties or restrictive conditions not imposed on other members of the community, it is discriminatory.

Mr. Justice McIntyre went on at pp. 549–50 [D/3106, para. 24768] to explain the rationale for this conclusion as follows:

To take the narrower view and hold that intent is a required element of discrimination under the
Code
would seem to me to place a virtually insuperable barrier in the way of a complainant seeking a remedy. It would be extremely difficult in most circumstances to prove motive, and motive would be easy to cloak in the formation of rules which, though imposing equal standards, could create, as in
Griggs
v.
Duke Power Co.,
401 U.S. 424 (1971), injustice and discrimination by the equal treatment of those who are unequal (
Dennis
v.
United States,
339 U.S. 162 (1950), at p. 184). Furthermore, as I have endeavoured to show, we are dealing here with consequences of conduct rather than with punishment for misbehaviour. In other words, we are considering what are essentially civil remedies. The proof of intent, a necessary requirement in our approach to criminal and punitive legislation, should not be a governing factor in construing human rights legislation aimed at the elimination of discrimination.

Issue

[
60
]    The issue to be determined by this Board of Inquiry is whether the School Board has discriminated against the complainant and his children contrary to para. (b) of
s. 5(1)
of the
Act
which has been quoted earlier. Paragraph (a) of
s. 5(1)
prohibits discrimination with respect to access to accommodation, services or facilities that are available to the public. Paragraph (b) of
s. 5(1)
extends the prohibition regarding discrimination beyond mere denial of initial access to ensure that once accessed any aspect of the accommodation, services or facilities provided are not distinguishable on the basis of any of the discriminatory grounds identified in
s. 5(1)
.

[
61
]    There are several preliminary questions relating to the applicability of s. 5 which must be addressed before any conclusions with respect to the merits of the complaint can be reached.

Whether the Board of Inquiry is the Proper Forum

[
62
]    An argument was raised that this Board of Inquiry is not the proper forum for the resolution of the issue before it. It was argued that it should be addressed through provisions in the collective agreement and the
Public Service Labour Relations Act,
R.S.N.B. 1973, c. P-25, that allow a school board to discipline a teacher for just cause and provide a grievance and adjudication process through which a teacher can challenge the appropriateness of disciplinary action. As referred to in the evidence, the employer has taken disciplinary action against Malcolm Ross on at least two occasions for reasons partially related to the issue before this Board of Inquiry. It was argued that labour relations would become a nightmare if disputes between a school board and teachers could be brought before a board of inquiry as well as processed through the grievance and adjudication process.

[
63
]    It is possible that the actions of a teacher that have been the subject of disciplinary action by an employer could come before an adjudicator and at the same time be before a board of inquiry as a result of a complaint under human rights legislation. There is no guarantee that in such a case priority will be given by the School Board to the requirements and objectives of the
Human Rights Act.
In such cases it is clear that the primary jurisdiction to address complaints alleging breaches of the human rights legislation is that of a board of inquiry. The collective agreement itself in art. 12 makes reference to the supremacy of legislation over the collective agreement. This basic principle, that the parties to a collective agreement cannot contract out of human rights legislation, is also supported in the Supreme Court of Canada decision
Re Winnipeg School Division No. 1 and Craton

(1985),
1985 CanLII 48 (SCC)
,
21 D.L.R. (4th) 1
[6 C.H.R.R. D/3014]. See also:
Ontario Human Rights Commission
v.
Borough of Etobicoke

(1982),
1982 CanLII 15 (SCC)
,
40 N.R. 159
[3 C.H.R.R. D/781] (S.C.C.).

[
64
]    Counsel for the Teachers' Federation expressed concern that to allow such matters to come before a board of inquiry would create a watershed of complaints and be very disruptive of the traditional manner of handling such issues through adjudication. There is no evidence to suggest that this would be the case. However, even if this was to occur, it would not allow a board of inquiry to relinquish its primary jurisdiction to deal with alleged violations of the
Act
.

Whether Public Education in the Public Schools is a Service

[
65
]    One preliminary issue which has already been addressed by the courts is whether the public education system in the public schools of New Brunswick falls within the scope of
s. 5
as being an accommodation, services or facilities available to the public. In its decision [
Board of Euducation of District 15
],
supra,
at p. 202 [D/6431, para. 45418] the New Brunswick Court of Appeal concluded as follows:

When one gives to Subsection 5(1) of the Act a "fair, large and liberal interpretation" as required by
Section 17
of the
Interpretation Act,
R.S.N.B. 1973, c. I-13, it would, I think, undoubtedly bring public education within its purview. To hold otherwise would seem to me to frustrate the legislative intent of the
Human Rights Act
and its preamble and amount to a rejection of the broad purposive approach to the interpretation of anti-discrimination legislation adopted by the Supreme Court of Canada.

More specifically, at pp. 203–4 the Court of Appeal concluded that public education provided under the
Schools Act,
R.S.N.B. 1973, c. S-5, is a service available to the public. This Board of Inquiry, therefore, has received direction from the New Brunswick Court of Appeal that
s. 5
of the
Act
does apply to the provision of public educational services by the various school boards in the province of New Brunswick.

Whether the School Board is a Person for Purposes of Section 5

[
66
]    A second preliminary issue that must be answered is whether the School Board is a person, as referred to in
s. 5
, that is capable of discriminating against other persons with respect to the accommodation, services or facilities available to the public. The definition of person as set out in the
Act
is not very helpful. It merely states that in addition to the extended meaning given to this word by the
Interpretation Act
,
it includes an employment agency, an employer's organization and a trade union. The
Interpretation Act,
R.S.N.B. 1973, c. I-13, s. 38, defines "person" as follows:

"Person" or "party" includes a corporation, partnership or society and the heirs, executors, administrators or other legal representatives of a person.

[
67
]    There would seem to be no doubt that a school board established under the
Schools Act
of New Brunswick is a person for purposes of the
Act
.
It first of all may be fairly implied from the decision of the Court of Appeal, although it is not specifically addressed. To find otherwise would, of course, largely defeat the application of
s. 5
to public education under the
Schools Act
as many decisions taken with respect to policy and programs that may result in discrimination are decisions by a school board rather than individuals.

[
68
]    The argument was raised by counsel that because the term "employer" is specifically referred to in s. 3(1) of the
Act
the legislators must not have intended for the School Board, as an employer, to be included in the term "person." This conclusion does not follow from a reading of s. 3(1) which states:

3. (1) No employer, employers' organization or other person acting on behalf of an employer shall

(a)   refuse to employ or continue to employ any person, or

(b)   discriminate against any person in respect of employment or any term or condition of employment,

because of race, colour, religion, national origin, ancestry, place of origin, age, physical disability, mental disability, marital status or sex.

First of all, as
s. 3
is specifically addressing discrimination in employment, it is logical that the "employer" should be specifically identified in this section. Secondly, the phrase "or other person" is used in conjunction with the term "employer" and implies that an employer does fall within the more general term "person" as used in other sections of the
Act
including
s. 5
. A similar conclusion was reached in relation to a similar argument raised with respect to the Newfoundland
Human Rights Code
[
1988,
S.N. 1988, c. 62]
in the case of
Memorial University of Newfoundland
v.
Rose

(1990),
1989 CanLII 4934 (NL SC)
,
80 Nfld. & P.E.I.R. 97 (S.C.T.D.)
. In that case it was argued by Memorial University that an employer did not fall within the scope of s. 10.2(1) of the
Human Rights Code
because it was not a "person" as contemplated by that section. The court found the section did apply to the university.

Whether Complainant is a Person for Purposes of Section 5

[
69
]    A further preliminary question to be resolved is whether the complainant, David Attis, having filed the complaint, falls within the category of persons whom
s. 5
was intended to protect. The New Brunswick Court of Appeal [
Board of Education of District 15
],
supra,
at p. 206 [D/6432], concluded that David Attis met the statutory standard in
s. 17
to be accorded the legal status of complainant. It further recognized that the major intent of his complaint was " . . . that the School Board has discriminated against him and his children." It seems clear that as a parent of children in School District 15 that his connection to and personal interest in the educational services provided by the School Board are closely linked to those of his children. As a parent he must assume certain legal and family responsibilities thus permitting a conclusion that he can claim to be an aggrieved person pursuant to
s. 17
of the
Act
.
David Attis is entitled to file the complaint not only in his own right but also on behalf of his children. Further, David Attis and his children are followers of the Jewish religion and are of Jewish ancestry, the two grounds on which they allege the discrimination was based.

Whether Section 6 Restricts the Scope of Section 5

[
70
]    Another argument of a preliminary nature challenged that
s. 6(2)
of the
Act
restricts the scope of
s. 5
of the
Act.

Subsection 6(2)
provides as follows:

6. (2) Nothing in this section interferes with, restricts, or prohibits the free expression of opinions upon any subject by speech or in writing.

It was argued that
s. 6(2)
prevents the application of
s. 5
to situations in which teachers are exercising their right to freely express their opinions as was Malcolm Ross through his published writings and public statements. This argument is rejected for several reasons. Firstly, it is noted that in
s. 6(2)
the reference is to nothing in "this section" prohibiting the free expression of opinion. If it was intended for this exemption clause to have broader application, it would have stated that nothing in "this
Act
" interferes, restricts or prohibits the free expression of opinions.

[
71
]    A review of decisions in other jurisdictions where there are similar provisions in human rights legislation supports the conclusion that equivalent provisions to s. 6(2) have not been applied beyond the scope of the section within which they were found. To apply
s. 6(2)
to other provisions of the
Act
would substantially restrict and limit the applicability of these sections contrary to the broad purposive approach to interpretation which the courts have adopted. If for example, to follow the argument,
s. 6(2)
applied to limit s. 5(1), a teacher would be free to express any opinion in class or elsewhere regardless of how discriminatory it might be as long as it could be classified as the free expression of opinion by that teacher. Such a conclusion could not have been intended by the Legislature.

Whether Section 3 Restricts the Scope of Section 5

[
72
]    An argument was raised by counsel that to order the School Board to impose any restriction on Malcolm Ross's right to publish and express his ideas could be seen as a breach by the School Board of s. 3(1). Subsection 3(1), which has been quoted earlier, prohibits an employer from discriminating against any person in respect of employment because of religion. It should be noted that there was no evidence presented by Malcolm Ross that his religion requires him to write in the manner that he has written. His writings suggest that he is writing out of some religious conviction but there was no direct evidence of this and no argument made as to his beliefs meeting the tenets of any particular religion. However, in the event that the conclusion of this Board of Inquiry is incorrect as to there being insufficient evidence to prove that Malcolm Ross's writings are required by his religion, it is necessary to address the relationship between
s. 3
and
s. 5
.

[
73
]    Both s. 3 and s. 5 provide protection against discrimination on the basis of religion. Therefore, it is possible that a situation could exist where the legitimate expression of a religious belief by one individual could breach another individual's right to be protected from discrimination on the basis of religion. In such a case it would be necessary to reach a reasonable balance between the two rights. In determining the balance, it is useful to consider the case of
Boucher
v.
The King,

1950 CanLII 2 (SCC)
,
[1951] S.C.R. 265
, at 277
where Rinfret J., in dissent, in considering the scope of freedom of expression stated:

. . . to interpret freedom as licence is a dangerous fallacy. Obviously pure criticism, or expression of opinion, however severe or extreme, is, I might almost say, to be invited. But, as was said elsewhere, "there must be a point where restriction on individual freedom of expression is justified and required on the grounds of reason, or on the ground of the democratic process and the necessities of the present situation."
